title: Universal text macro for all inbox messages and setting patient expectations
content:
Hey all,

Like everyone else I am exhausted in part due to the excessive inbox workload. Constant messages, requests for free care (“can’t you just send me in an antibiotic?”), questions, unfiltered trains of thought from patients, and unnecessary health updates. 

I pretty much always say “this needs a visit” in a nice way to each message, but even that is wearing me down. 

I’ve been thinking about making a universal text macro for all inbox messages. Something along the lines of:

“This is an automated message. Due to high demand I am unfortunately unable to answer individual portal messages. If you have an immediate concern please contact our phone triage system. If you have an emergency please go to the ED. Otherwise please schedule a visit with me at your convenience to discuss your questions or concerns. Thank you for your understanding. I look forward to speaking soon.” 

I’m very tired of patients wanting concierge medicine for free.

I’m also considering giving a handout at the establishing visit to help set expectations. Something to summarize professionally that visits are only for a set amount of time and if you are late then it comes out of your visit time, only covering a 2-3 things per visit, no patient portal messages, if you need a refill you need a visit, if you need a referral you need a visit, maintaining a culture of mutual respect and professionalism, etc.

Has anyone done either of these things? Any advice for or against?

Thanks

comments.body:
As someone obsessed with optimizing our finite time in medicine, here’s a better solution:

Prevent the message from arriving into your inbox in the first place. Unless your EMR can automatically send out your message, this reduces the amount of input to your inbox which ultimately requires an output (you having to send a message to patients, your MA, your nurse, etc)

Here are suggestions how:

-Do not encourage portal usage, tell patients and your team to nudge towards office appts.

-Do not respond to non urgent messages immediately (don’t create the expectation of immediate answers).

-Do not be the initial receiver of the message, have your practice route message first to your MA, triage nurse, front desk depending on type.

-Disable “reply” when sending a message to a patient.

-If you anticipate having to review labs/imaging, make them schedule follow up appointment at check out (likely already happening for most).

-Choose a limit per patient (I.e. if more than 2 messages are sent by a patient or more than 100-150 words are in the message then it’s automatically an appointment).

These are just a few options.


REMEMBER: Eliminate, automate, delegate, collaborate


EDIT:
Check out these sources:

AAFP Techniques to Reduce EHR Inbox Burden: https://www.aafp.org/family-physician/practice-and-career/administrative-simplification/ehr-inbox/techniques-ehr-burden.html

AMA Managing the EHR inbox takes a system. Here’s how to set one up: https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/digital-health/managing-ehr-inbox-takes-system-here-s-how-set-one

replies.body: There are lots of potential boundaries to set but at the end of the day many docs are at the mercy of the policy where they work when it comes to how to deal w MyChart messages. It’s funny the number of pts who’ve remarked to me that doctors must love MyChart (I guess they assume it’s better than the old days of having to return phone calls).

title: Patients calling and expecting to speak with the doctor/provider and not the clinic staff
content:
*Disclaimer: I am an RN in an outpatient specialty office rather than family med. There are very few outpatient nurses in the nursing sub, so I figured this would resonate more here. If this doesn't fit here, please feel free to delete. 😊

In my office, we have recently seen an increase in patients who call the office and expect to speak directly to my doctor. If it's a voicemail, it's "This is Mary Patient and I would like Dr. Doctor to call me back, I have a question". If it's a direct phone conversation, it's "Just let me talk to Dr. Doctor, I don't want to talk to you". It's happening enough that we're all noticing it and we're wondering why this is happening.

I've been with my doctor for 8 years and this is NEVER how it's been in our office. That's not to say he never is on the phone with patients, but it's always been the nursing/clinical staff who answer the phones, triage symptoms, take the information, and either we provide the answer ourselves or we speak directly to or get a message to the doctor (he has hospital shifts where he's covering inpatient floors or the unit, so he's in the office every other week). We then call the patient back and relay his recommendations. If it's a complex patient or situation, he will occasionally call them back himself, but it's usually one of us calling the patient back.

Are other offices seeing this kind of thing, or are our patients just weird? For context, we are not a concierge practice, we are not a private practice. We are affiliated with a hospital system, we follow their general phone policies plus our own office phone policies.

🤷🏼‍♀️

comments.body:
Primary care RN here:  Legit

Explain that the provider is in an appt and they want us to pull them out.  Explain that the person in the appointment reserved that time with their provider so I'd be happy to schedule you...NO.  Well if you tell me what's going on maybe the virtual team will be able to....NO.

The entitlement is crazy.

replies.body:
Primary care here too. And same!

No I will not go interrupt another patient’s scheduled appointment time. The entitlement is heavy now. I feel having the port has given some patients a feeling of constant access to their providers who definitely are not viewed as humans. I had a patient snap at me because their PCP is out of office for a ‘family emergency’ (death of their spouse which we obviously aren’t sharing with patients) and I wouldn’t call them for the patient.

Neurosurgery clinic RN here. “He’s in surgery. No I don’t know how long he’ll be in surgery. No I’m not going down to the hospital to break into the OR to put him on speakerphone. No I don’t know how long he’ll be in surgery.”

title: Prognosis of Primary Care
content:
**TLDR: Another fun burnout post, wondering how we are doing dealing with admin burden + worried for the future of primary care** 

As I sit with a fat stack of paperwork and endless inbasket to manage on this Friday night, I've been pondering (all week): where is our career field going? 

Feels like we are saddled with an astronomical administrative burden and at least where I work, we are magically supposed to take care of it all and make it all go away in our (uncompensated) free time- a la Houdini.  I chose my job for scheduling freedom and seemingly, for lifestyle/work-like balance. This has turned out to be a total joke as I have zero admin time and am pure productivity based. I have an affluenza/geriatric/entitled elderly patient base that I inherited from a retiring PCP who are used to same day messaging and responses- basically, concierge level care. Many patients were directed to establish with our sister clinics to share the burden, but so many have weasled their way back into our site because “\[they\] are paying customers and why should they have to go somewhere else?” and a plethora of other BS reasoning. My clinic has now lost two more PCP’s, one of which retired in their early 50’s, and patients are perplexed- “Why did Dr. XYZ leave? He was too young!”

I can tell you why he retired. Because of \*gestures everywhere\* THIS. Panel overload. No accessibility. Endless paperwork, disability, exploding inbaskets. Never-ending, sky-rocketing expectations that we PCP’s can remain Atlas, condemned to hold up the healthcare world as it crumbles around us. We have MA’s only, no RN’s (red flag #1) because we can’t afford them. While clinicians have fairly good control over appointment times/scheduling, the inverse is that our support is severely lacking…even with a virtual team to cut down on inbasket burden. The admin burden volume I need to deal with daily remains untenable and literally none of the older docs I work with seem mentally well.  

I read these magical sounding posts with docs saying they put it 0 time on inbasket outside of clinic. HOW?! I do 1.5-2 hours per day and it still isn’t enough. I have to catch up every weekend. And this is with a reasonable patient load (max 18 patients per day, usually 15ish…but complex and old). Is it my entitled patients? Lack of RN? Point is moot. I feel almost depersonalized at this point. I did not go into medicine to spend hours and hours and hours on inbasket and administrative BS. My office leadership has no desire to change things and has repeatedly said “this is how modern primary care is, suck it up” which I find insane. I feel like an indentured servant, not a physician.  Working on the concept of radical acceptance, and moving into accepting my current reality (because I have an active escape plan), but overall I am wondering this: what are we going to do when the bough breaks? 

I feel that today’s newly-minted primary care docs are getting the extreme short end of the stick. Relatively stagnating pay, all of the liability, none of the autonomy, and ever-increasing patient demands + administrative burden + complex medicine in the aging population where we are continually dumped on and expected to manage more and more and do less with less due to specialists also being overwhelmed. 

Most of my friends are crispy burnt out and making plans to leave primary care and I can't blame them. I am one of them. Perhaps limitless boundary setting (every visit, every day, every message, for forever) and fighting admin is the answer, but this is my second awful experience working as a PCP- and I am just exhausted and done. 

This is peak burn out but also curious to hear other opinions.

comments.body:
Listen. This sounds rough and no way I’d want to work that much.  I sympathize.  I also think your practice sounds like part of the problem. With multiple providers and an elderly, affluent population.  You should absolutely be able to afford nurses, unless someone is preferring to pull out the nursing salary as profit for themselves?  

Nurses are vital to managing admin, portal and burn out in my experience.    It sounds like you may also need to break a few eggs with patients.  I took over from an old doc who had a similar lack of boundaries.  I made it clear with patients that my standards were going to be different and I did not respond to portal messages with anything other than yes, no or book an appointment.  Some patients left ( and I will not miss them at all).  Most got used to it and I’m doing way better a couple years down the line.   It’s especially important book appointments if you’re productivity based. If you’re spending more than 5 minutes on something for a patient outside a visit it needs to be a visit.   You’ve got to start billing for and scheduling the work you do so it doesn’t take up your life outside work.  


If your job isn’t supportive of making changes, hiring nurses or you running your panel the way you want to it’s time to seek another job.  There are plenty of reasonable options out there.  Unfortunately there are also a lot of places that will work your the bone and convince you it’s the norm or you just aren’t doing enough.   It sounds like you may be at o wood those places and it might be time to bail.

title: Testing Requests
content:
In addition to the absolutely absurd amount of nonsense that patients request on the regular during actual appointments, are we now somehow expected to respond to the flood of requests via MyChart either to upcoming visits or post-visit add-ons??

Is this too harsh as a response?
“Appropriate, evidence-based testing was ordered at time of visit. Further testing requests are welcome to evidence-based discussions at any future appointments.”
(tldr: I will not be adding on your T3 for no reason, ma’am; you’ve been stable on your thyroid replacement for years…)

Some of these people would be much better suited to some concierge (or functional) medicine in their lives….

comments.body:
As most others have said, any “extension of the appointment,” lab tests, or new medications/ medication adjustments that weren’t discussed in the visit are told to come in for an office visit.

I had a new patient recently asking about increasing the dose of a medication we had just started the week prior and I told her that I would like to hold off on any medication changes as we had a follow up 4 weeks out from the original appointment. 

MyChart isn’t e-medicine, it’s a way to ask a quick question, not a place to discuss medical management. If you set this boundary to your patients they will quickly learn. And those that are unhappy will leave.

replies.body: “MyChart isn’t e-medicine” - this is a fantastic point

setting boundaries is really important. 

I recently covered the inbox for a older colleague who has been in practice for decades, the volume of requests he gets for shit is insane, and the kinds of requests often require extensive MDM. it was eye opening because I never get those kinds of messages because my panel is has expectations set a certain way, but the kinds of stuff his panel is obviously accustomed to being managed on the portal was absurd

What is your phrasing for these “extension of visit” things, because this is where my boundaries are the most loosely goosey. I try, but often spend so much time boundary-setting, that I might as well have done what they were asking (which would have been 10x quicker).

title: How many patients/day are we "supposed" to handle?
content:
This is something I've been pondering as a new attending. I've seen a wide spectrum of docs from across the world saying how many patients they see.

I've heard docs talk about how their average day is 25-30+ patients a day. While others say they handle 12-14 tops, giving them time to complete other work.

Right now, I have 18-21 patients a day, and I'm getting done on time and able to knock out the notes reasonably efficiently, but the inbasket is kicking my ass. Demands for phone calls (free visits), medication demands, bucketloads of paperwork (who knew trying to get 2 weeks off from Walmart requires 5 separate forms), constant mychart messages (followed by a "DID YOU SEE MY MESSAGE" because my network promises a response in 48 hours), etc. It's ridiculous.

I am trying to wrap my head around what we are supposed to be capable of. How do docs seeing 30+ patients a day do it? Is there a more optimal strategy/approach I'm ignorant to?

I feel stupid complaining about my 18-21 patients/day schedule when other docs are handling 30+, but I am barely keeping pace, sitting up now at 10PM still doing inbasket/notes. At work, there's extremely little downtime too. Not like I'm twiddling my thumbs most of the day. It's all movement. I seem to absorb all the SDS visits right now, including a 15 minute acute chest pain, crammed in new patient HFU visits, etc. Nothing I can't handle but it's constant- there is never downtime.

While I think my health network is "decent", many FM docs quit, go concierge, go do fellowships, fight tooth-and-nail to do part time or reduce their hours from 36 to 32 patient-facing hours, etc. My office has been hemorrhaging multiple docs, so despite thinking my network is "decent"... it can't be that great. There's a doc just a few years older and he's talking to a lawyer to get a part-time clause forced into his next contract. The only true, solid dependable docs in the office are an old doc on the cusp of retirement (he helped found the place) and a very depressed and unhealthy middle aged doc who seems miserable all-the-time. The guy that wants part time is very quick to get confrontational with the manager, and the depressed middle-aged doc often jokingly threatens the manager she will quit. Is that normal? All the FM docs back in my residency, being in a residency program, only have to see like.... 7-9 patients..... 3 days a week.... so they don't really have this perspective.

I kinda just want to hear other people's perspectives. Get some insight and grounding into if I'm naive/ignorant/spoiled/lost in my view on things (if I'm the stereotypical self-important millenial who unjustly thinks he is owed the world), or if I'm getting the shit end of the stick and I don't see it fully. I'm in the Philadelphia area, so I'm getting paid like 220k to have 36 patient hours, 18-21 patients a day on full days. Not sure how this stacks up.

comments.body: I’m in the same boat as you. 18-21 typically scheduled. I know my limits. I’ve had days where only 16-17 show and I still feel like I had a long day dealing with patients, paperwork, inbox etc. Overall I can manage it but it’s non-stop from the moment I step in my office until I leave every day. I don’t have a clue how people see 25-30 AND deal with all of the additional responsibilities.

replies.body: I'm right there with you. I just don't get it. Hell, I could see even more patients if it was just seeing patients and belting out some notes. But the inbasket easily demands several hours a day. Maybe our networks over-emphasize the inbasket as a way of improving 'customer satisfaction' at the major cost of efficiency?

My motivation to see 30 patients per day is to get enough cash flow to retire early. Invest early, invest frequenly, retire Early. My goal is to exit this career as soon as possible, primary care is fucking stupid.

title: DPC summit
content: I'm currently at the DPC summit.  I can tell already, there are some physicians who are going to turn in their letter of resignation when they get back. I want to highlight this model but this is not the only way to find happiness in your career. Be willing to break the mold. I want you walk a different path because the status quo is unacceptable. I'm energized right now and wanted to offer a word of  encouragement.

comments.body: Two biggest drawbacks in my uneducated opinion. I don't want entitled patients having MORE access to me. I don't want a patient population who can "afford to pay my services". If a patient doesn't have enough money to have a DPC doctor, are they out of luck?

replies.body: Probably depends on the practice but the nice thing would be you have the choice since you don’t have to be dictated to by insurance. Could barter with them or just do it for free

Your issue 1 and issue 2 have the same answer, it’s your practice and your decision. If patient sucks and is legit abusing privileges, YOU DECIDE when and if you keep taking care of them. 

Same thing about price, you decide what to charge and who gets special lower pricing, as long as you are smart with finances you can allocate 10% of panel to charity or lower socioeconomic status patients. Charge them 30$ or something along those lines to ensure patients still value services and you  preserve their dignity. People value a good bargain more than freebies. 

Ultimately you set the rules and you change them as you see fit

title: Manipulating your schedule/follow-ups/etc?
content:
In corporate traditional primary care, one of the few things we lowly physicians have control over is when/if our patients follow up.

Is your office jamming new est patients into your schedule? Schedule everyone for 2-3 month follow ups to blockade it.

Are you getting tons of volume that you don't want? Schedule follow ups for patients you know to be unreliable and won't show.

Cellulitis. "Better check that in 2 days" Abscess. Whatever. Come back for a "wound check." (a nice break in the schedule)...

I've never really consciously done these things, but it's entered my mind and I can see how it happens. Had an older attending at a practice once whose schedule was literally nothing but "2 month follow-up" right down the board, non-diabetics, elderly, utterly useless appointments (except maybe in the patients' non-informed minds). He protected himself well from the corporation, though I don't think did much good for the community, and I guess corporate was totally fine with this proce$$.....

EDIT: to clarify, I do NOT do this. And in fact I'm not even in corporate traditional PCP land anymore. I own a DPC and med spa. But I still think back to the hamster-wheel days...

comments.body:
I think like all things nothing is black and white. I work in a VBC model so that frames my thinking a it too.

Monthly follow up for my patient with stable (but still active) schizophrenia? Yes because i truly believe shooting the shit with him and saying CPM once a month helps remind him we’re here for him and helps keep him out of the ER. He still has magical delusions but they’re never violent (anymore). So I think that standing visit helps him and helps me pad my schedule with an easy visit. And I recognize full well if he decompensates that I am prepared for a tough visit  

Making up a fake patient ? That’s pretty unethical. Can’t see any way around it. 

Scheduling a flakey patient knowing they’ll likely no-show? That’s more gray to me. If they should be following up then by all means. If you’re doing it solely for the potential free time then 

In the end I think medicine has been corporatized and we as physicians and providers need to advocate for ourselves because that ultimately is what affects our patients. Do I feel bad not squeezing in an extra patient when I’m pressured to? At times, but that feeling passes quick when I remember for every time we let that slip, some corporate overlord gets the idea we can more work in less time and soon enough we’re all seeing 20+ patients a day and practicing poorer quality medicine

title: FM as an outsider - learning to work in a clinic
content:
IANAFMD.

I am not boarded in FM. Currently boarded and practicing as an EM attending, for about 10 years. I have been slowly and methodically planning my exit from EM through sports medicine, and I'll be applying for fellowship in Primary Care Sports Medicine this summer/cycle. I'm a little bit terrified of clinic work because of how much I dont know/have forgotten. I masquerade as a PCP to some of my patients, because they won't/can't/don't see a true PCP. But I know where my weaknesses are, trust me. 

If you were wanting to work in an ED, I'd gladly take on the challenge, and help you out. In my mind, you need to know how to deal with crashing patients, and be adept at procedures. Those things I'm good at. 

If I wanted to come and work in a clinic as an EM trauma center doctor, what are my big weaknesses going to be? What books or conferences can I start investigating/using to be better for my patients. I know that nothing I do will replace an FM residency, but I want to be better for my patients. Which direction would you point me for learning? 

I'd like to consider a DPC style clinic maybe with hybrid sports medicine in the future; what will make me not look like an idiot to my FM/clinic based peers and to the specialists I'll work with? I know there isn't an easy/quick answer, but I want to try and put in the work now to help me amd my patients later. 

Thoughts?

PS - EM=/=FM boards. I get that. ED docs can't just work in a clinic because it's slower and they can 'figure it out.' What you guys do is an art that I dont know about. Learn me your ways, I'm here to absorb. I've been reading through the FM subreddit for at least 6 months or more, you guys are civil and realistic over here, and you seem to like your jobs. Most of the EM forums here and SDN are pretty rowdy and hate filled. I think we hate our choices and don't know how to fix it as a whole.

comments.body: I'd say being comfortable waiting is the biggest learning. You can't just order imaging on the whim and "know" the diagnosis right away or consult a specialist same day. You have to be comfortable waiting for results and following up.  It might be a while for someone knows exactly what is going on or insurance approves xyz.  I was at one didactics where the EM doc and pharmacists were trashing GLP-1s because of "all the side effects" they were seeing in the ED.  Well I got news: they are our best drugs and most patients have minimal side effects so put the hospital bias aside and actually do what is right for the patient. Furthermore, be comfortable prescribing stuff people are going to say "what the hell is the PCP doing" because sometimes that's all the patient is willing to take or insurance will pay for.  I see this with hospitalists saying things like "consider xyz outpatient for better control" on discharge notes. Yep bud thanks for the advice lol. Honestly, I'd be down for a 1 year fellowship for EM to transition to FM similar to FM having a 1 year to EM fellowship.  The mindsets are definitely different though as chronic disease management takes time and is not immediate.

replies.body:
I think the waiting will be the weird part. Rearranging my brain to still consider the what ifs without going after them all the time. So many patients I see as a nocturnist have no business being in the ED, but they are the worried well, or they can't see their PCP for 4-6 weeks and they don't want to wait. Or they have an appointment in the morning and 'just couldn't wait.' ::rolleyes:: I have a few partners that always seem to trash or give other specialties a hard time, and I never understood it. Your comment about not caring what others think because that may be all the patient can get or afford is heard, loud and clear. I just want to make sure I'm starting out in the right direction. 
I know I'll have to get things approved through insurance for the sports med clinic, and that will be a bummer and frustration. It's my understanding with DPC clinics though that they don't bill or utilize insurance at all, is that correct? I know a few of the concierge practicies around us charge a retainer as well as utilizing insurance, so thats not quite what I'm gunning for. 
I've got a bit of reading to do on chronic disease management. Thanks for the direction!
They have the FM to EM except no one will hire you. Make it the other way around and you’d get hired instantly

title: Direct Primary Care
content:
Apologies is this is the wrong place to post this… I’m a dentist who lurks here to learn from you all—many of your patient issues look like mine, surprisingly.

How do you feel about direct primary care? I’m considering becoming a DPC patient because I realized I feel like my no-insurance patients receive more nuanced care than my insurance pts (i.e. fewer delays, more transparency in pricing, etc.). I want those things, too, and heaven knows primary care is a hellscape of unnecessary hoops to jump through. And, I want to know my provider is getting paid a reasonable amount to spend time talking with me about my health.

What should I, as a fellow healthcare provider, know about transitioning to DPC? (I’ll still have health insurance.) Any red flags to worry about when choosing an office/provider? Pros/cons I may not be considering?

Thank you to you guys for everything you do. I genuinely respect the work you do for my patients!

comments.body: I think it’s worth it if you have a lot of issues and need more time with primary care.

title: Subreddit State of the Union 2024
content:
# Another year, another annual mod update!

Thank you everyone for all the contributions and growth of this community over the past year - we've almost doubled in size, and it's been really great to see how the subreddit has changed over the years. Below is a summary of the most recent developments, works in process and hopes for upcoming projects. And as always, we welcome feedback from you all about what you want to see/don't want to see for the subreddit.

**- mandatory user flair:** added earlier this year to distinctly display a person's job status (MD/DO/resident/RN/layperson etc) and has cut significantly down on spam and non-medical persons posting! If you have a specific request for user flair not currently listed, message mods.

**- optional verified user flair:** want to show your flair as verified? [Click here](https://www.reddit.com/r/FamilyMedicine/wiki/index/) to read how to apply for verified user flair in the Wiki. Also can [click here](https://www.reddit.com/r/FamilyMedicine/comments/18rqxgq/important_mod_update_user_flair/) for a post with FAQ about user flair.

**- expanded wiki resource:** on the right sidebar, the wiki contains info about the subreddit moderation standards, applicant resources, residency topics including exams, and a career tab that is in process but currently includes a FAQ about DPC practice.

**- trimonthly jobs & career thread:** had heard multiple times that the # of career posts was getting a bit excessive on the main page, everyone voted to have a stickied thread to collate the posts while also leaving career posts on the main page. So we now have 2 stickied posts (which is our maximum), one for students and one for job posts. It's not used very frequently, I have some hope that this will catch on but honestly it doesn't seem to be, is usually empty, and will likely be phased out some point over the next several months if it doesn't pick up steam. (There are other things I'd like to have in a stickied post, things much more exciting, as below).

**- what is continuing to be worked on/ideas for future:** expanding career resources and info, start some sort of advocacy in FM resource, establish a schedule of AMA's on variety of topics (different practice models, AMA with recruiter, FM/OB AMA, rural practice AMA, etc). Goal for the year is set up a recurring AMA event. If you're interested in doing an AMA, message mods!! Would love to hear if there is interest.

Cheers to the next year, and thank you to everyone who finds any source of community here, whether by posts, comments, or just stalking the page as a silent participant and reader.

comments.body: Thanks all, this is a good sub

title: Addiction Med Q&A
content:
I have had a good number of people reach out to me expressing interest and asking questions about Addiction Medicine.  Bear in mind that I'm just a PGY-5 FM MD in the mid-west.  One of the best things about AdMed IMO is that any specialty can put it into practice and the variability even within a specialty can be dramatic.  Would love to hear other addiction docs' input and feedback, so please feel free to have at it.

Apologies for the length and redundancy, but I just don't have the time or energy to post a polished long-form product right now.  My plan is to come back to this and continue to edit/add to it.  Will do my best to answer other questions in comments too.

Cheers!

P.S. u/darthbeeman wrote up [a fantastic post detailing his journey](https://www.reddit.com/r/AddictionMedicine/comments/1497rwf/addiction_medicine_practice_pathway_education_and/) through the process as well. Highly recommend checking that out for more reading.

——————————————————————————————

**User1**

Hey! What is Job outlook like now addiction Med? Any info on salary numbers?

**abertheham**

Job outlook is open to whatever you want to do with it, i.e. it depends on what proportion of your time and practice you want to commit to it. I work mostly in primary care and take internal referrals from colleagues to provide outpatient treatment and/or evals to funnel patients into higher levels of care. But some people choose to work exclusively in addiction, in settings like inpatient treatment facilities, hospital consultation services, detox centers, and OTPs. The field is still new so the possibilities are largely open to your imagination and networking opportunities.

Salary is going to be dependent on which of those contexts you choose to work in, but is largely based on your primary board certification.

**User1**

Do you have any advice on what to do to improve CV if looking to go into addiction Med?

**abertheham**

Depends on the program, but most of them are not super competitive. The past few years there haven't been enough applicants to fill all the fellowships, so it's not like you need to really impress on paper. I'd say a good personal statement will take you a lot further. Being genuine in your desire to care for people and improve your knowledge base will go a long ways.

It wouldn't hurt to have publications, QI projects, volunteering experience that shows some predilection toward working with use disorders, but I wouldn't say that's critical.

As I interviewed potential fellows last year, it felt like some applicants were doing addiction medicine and/or applying to our program just because it showed up in their list on ERAS. Programs are obviously going to want to know why you want to train with them specifically, so do your best to make that come through as well.

Sorry if that's not quite the answer you were looking for--happy to clarify or answer other questions

**User1**

Thank you so much!

What does it mean that people applied to your program just because you showed up on eras?

If geography is preference would that not show? Or I guess would have to show that in the personal statement?

In terms of competitiveness, I’ll be applying when they close the pathway so the only way to get certified is through fellowship. You don’t think it will get more competitive then?

**abertheham**

I just meant it seemed like they threw out applications because our program was in a list of available programs—had no prior ties or interest in the region, didn’t seem to know much about the program at all or really have any interest in the area or anything you know? Not necessarily a bad thing in itself but it’s just not a great look when you don’t have an answer to “what drew you to/motivated you to apply to this program”

Hard to say what will happen to the competitiveness. Where are you at in your training?

As it stands right now, the salary is mostly influenced by primary board certification and there’s still a lot of stigma around the field, so I don’t see it getting dramatically more competitive in the next 3-5 years

**User1**

Ah okay I see. How do you find out more about programs if they don’t have much listed on their site? I tried finding any fellowship residency fairs but was not successful in that.

Just started pgy2

And I am in FM now

Oh okay awesome! Thanks!

**abertheham**

That’s a good question and a fair point actually. I guess maybe calling or emailing to ask for details would be the best avenue if there’s not much online. Otherwise just showing curiosity and asking for those details during the interview while also showing interest in AdMed as a whole and/or the geographic region.

I think maybe what I was getting at was that we interviewed a couple who seemed strangely ambivalent about the whole endeavor and that just wasn’t a good look.

And congrats on getting through intern year. I always tell people, that was the real, actual turning point where it finally stopped getting progressively shittier in training. Always thought getting through MCAT and into med school would be the hard part, then it just got worse and harder until after intern year, it FINALLY started easing up a little. Different kinds stressors still existed for me no doubt but on the whole, it felt like that’s when things actually turned around for the better. I lost that “it’s bad now but it’s gonna get worse” mindset. Idk how your program is, but hopefully the rest of residency is good to you. It does eventually end so hang in there.

**User1**

Okay thank you! I see what you mean!

Thank you so much!! I really appreciate it!!

**abertheham** 

Any time!

**User2**

Hello! Saw your comment about addiction med, thanks for being open for some questions! I basically thought only after 2025 admed will require fellowship…right now i thought you only needed to take the test ? what’s the most exciting part of your day when directly related to admed? thanks so much

**abertheham**

Hey! Sure, it's my pleasure. I can't remember the exact dates of when things will change, but the short version is that the people who grandfathered into the training via non-fellowship routes can continue, but basically the only way to start down the path now is through a fellowship. I think. That was the only path that was relevant to me, so I don't know the ins and outs of the practice pathway route or anything like that. I'm like 99% sure you can't just sit for the board exam anymore though.

The most exciting part of my day is meeting people where they're at. Ad med gets a lot of eye-rolls and 'oh man I bet that's a difficult population' kind of reactions, but it's an incredibly fulfilling field. What a lot of people don't consider is that by the time someone with a use disorder is sitting in your specialty clinic, they really just want help. I really enjoy employing harm reduction techniques and the open discourse that can genuinely give people their lives back in an incredibly powerful way. Suboxone is an incredible medication and I just love getting people with OUD started on it.

It definitely comes with its own set of unique challenges, and some cases ultimately prove tragic/fatal, but yeah... high highs and low lows, ya know?

Its also nice to be the one people turn to when they don't know how to handle those tricky situations. The education part and working to end stigma is quite important as well--both with patients and colleagues.

And finally, I guess I'd say that I like walking around with the knowledge that I could ditch primary care and go do specialty work in pretty much any setting, and finding that job (or building it from scratch) will be a lot easier with the dual board certification.

**User2**

Wow these are all amazing considerations and insights. Thank you so much for your reply and may you continue to have the positive impact on the people’s live you touch, you are appreciated!

——————————————————————————————

**User3**

Hello! I saw a comment on reddit of yours about chill medical specialties and im looking into addiction med but I wanted to ask your thoughts about lifestyle and compensation?

**abertheham**

Hey, sorry I just got this and am about to go to bed but am happy to discuss whenever.

The “short” version is lifestyle can be what you make it, but it does depend on your primary specialty to some extent. Compensation tends to be more or less the same as your primary specialty - possibly less if it was a high-dollar specialty, or possibly slightly more if it’s an adjunctive part of your practice.

It’s still a relatively new field so there is not like a single “typical” pathway or work scenario. That flexibility affords a lot of possibilities for great work/life balance. Anything from research and clinical trials, to primary care, to methadone clinics and residential treatment facilities; pain clinics, palliative clinics… it kind of runs the gambit.

Compensation will pretty much always be adequate as a physician in the US, imo, but then I live fairly modestly (not \*that\* modestly though) and went into family practice, so my perspective is likely to be quite different than some of the super competitive subspecialties that aim to take it from 6 figures to 7…

**User3**

You’re all good! I would love to optimize compensation and the variety of practice setting now! I’m between addiction and sleep and leaning more towards addiction rn but what do you think? What type of practice setting do you do now?

**abertheham**

I’m obviously biased towards addiction, but sleep is interesting too.

I’m about to start my first big boy job in a primary clinic doing mostly FM but taking referrals for addiction treatment. Depending on demand that may expand to have dedicated addiction days, e-consults, or an addiction-only practice.

I enjoy FM and want to practice it initially at least, but I’m open to being drawn into a sub specialty if the work shows up (or if primary care goes all the way to shit).

**User3**

Hi! I realized we ve talked before! I do really want to practice addiction and grow full time eventually and I hope I’m able to build a good private practice model and I was wondering how job variety is and compensation is?

**abertheham**

Variety is great—you can do pretty much whatever you like with it. Some run outpatient addiction clinics, some do inpatient rehab/detox management, some do hospital consult/liaison, some run methadone clinics… Demand is high so you can sort of choose your own adventure so-to-speak.

Compensation is variable because it’s going to be heavily based on your primary board certification.

**User3**

I’d love to do a variety with outpatient and inpatient consults with managing rehab/detox centers!

But my primary certification is FM!

**abertheham**

That’s perfect, tbh.

**abertheham** 

Bit harder for peds or IM because addiction knows no boundaries. With an FM primary, you can manage addiction in everyone from pregnancy/neonatal through geriatrics.

Regardless, I’m not sure how much you’ve looked into the job market, but FM compensation isn’t anything to bat an eye at…

You can work 4 days a week in a city making 250k+ or work your ass off and make a half million going rural, doing DPC, or something. Either way, life is comfortable.

title: How certain were you about family medicine before you began medical school?
content:
I'm in the process of applying to medical school right now. I've been fortunate to receive an interview for a three year MD program that automatically places you into the school's FM residency upon completion. 

It's a great opportunity as it saves a lot of time and money. Also, I have been interested in family medicine for a long time. I love the flexibility it offers, from the various fellowships to the hospitalist option to starting your own DPC, etc. I love the value that a good family medicine physician provides to their community. I've also shadowed a family medicine physician at my university and could definitely see myself in such a role down the line. I would say that at this point, I am 90% certain about entering primary care in some capacity, and 70% sure about family medicine.

My questions is: when you were at my stage in the process, were you set on family med and would you have chosen to attend this program if you had the chance? Obviously an interview is just an interview, but I've been thinking so much about this opportunity lately that I wanted actual FM docs to weigh in. I'd appreciate any advice :)

comments.body: I was 100% sold on family med before med school and the school confirmed my wishes. In terms of residency…I would look at that residency as a separate entity and make sure it’s where you want to train and all. I had never heard of the town/residency I am at before med school and it was my first choice after hearing through an attending and doing an audition.

title: Resigned from a hospital owned PCP network, starting a DPC. I can add a blurb to the patient notification letters, what can/should I say?
content:
Instead of a vague "Dr. So and so is no longer with the practice" my owners have allowed me to add a paragraph to the notification letters sent out to my patients. I haven't been given nor asked for details about any restrictions on what I can say. I honestly won't mind if 0 patients follow me to DPC. I don't need volume, that's kind of the point (which comedically the higher ups don't understand, they want to keep the practice drowning in volume and for me to not leave taking even a drop of it off their hands). Anyway, I'd still like those patients who want to follow to be able to do so. 

Any ideas how I should word this?

comments.body: Check your contract on patient notification of your new practice.  My contract states that if I move to a new job, my current one will tell patients where I went if they ask.
